clue.text: Embroidery. — spoil it with a tiny mark

parts.note: to spoil a child is to pet or pamper it
taken as written
a point is a dot, a very small mark

explanation.surface: A warning that one small blot will ruin a piece of needlework.
explanation.definitionFit: Petit point is a fine needlework stitch worked on canvas, a kind of decorative sewing.

clue.text: With all due respect, to measure .

explanation.surface: The clue runs into the next one: to measure a river you need pegs.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs on into 2 down; read together they form one sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Pace, from Latin, is a polite way to disagree with someone; it also means to measure a distance by steps.

clue.text: … a river you need pegs

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: measuring a river requires pegs.
explanation.walkthrough: Continues 1 down. The Tees is a river in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tees is a river in north-east England; tees are also the small pegs golfers rest the ball on.

clue.text: Disorder a trait in a lot of one-party states

indicators.note: to disorder something is to jumble it up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Unrest is a common feature in many single-party countries.
explanation.definitionFit: A totalitarian regime is one where a single party holds total control of the state.

clue.text: Stout leader of expedition has honours heaped upon him

indicators.note: in a down clue, heaped upon means the honours come above, before, the next piece

parts.note: OBEs are British honours, Officer of the Order of the British Empire

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A portly expedition leader showered with awards.
explanation.definitionFit: Stout means fat, heavily built, the same as very overweight.

clue.text: When there's the least change, despite an alteration being made

indicators.note: an alteration being made signals that the letters before it are changed around

explanation.surface: A remark that very little changed although an alteration was carried out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'an' belongs to the anagram letters; only 'alteration being made' signals the rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Neap tides occur at the moon's quarters, when the rise and fall of the sea is smallest.

clue.text: Academic in favour of piano? Just the opposite, in favour of forte

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
f is the musical abbreviation for forte, loud

explanation.surface: A musical teacher who, it turns out, likes loud playing rather than soft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In favour of piano' would be PRO + P (p = piano, soft); 'Just the opposite' swaps soft for loud, so the clue spells out the second version, PRO + F.
explanation.definitionFit: Prof is the short informal form of professor, a senior university teacher.

clue.text: Errant husband may meet this head-on

definitions.text: Errant husband may meet this head-on

parts.words: Errant husband may meet this head-on
parts.note: the cartoon image of a wife waiting up to hit a straying husband over the head with a kitchen tool

explanation.definitionFit: A rolling pin is the wooden roller for flattening pastry, the classic cartoon weapon of a wronged wife.

clue.text: The cost of conveying soldiers into battle before time

indicators.note: before means the battle piece comes ahead of the time piece
into means the soldiers are put inside the word for battle

parts.note: a fight is a battle
RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: The price of moving troops to the front before it is too late.
explanation.definitionFit: Freightage is the charge made for transporting goods.

clue.text: Mrs Sprat liked to grumble

explanation.surface: The nursery-rhyme wife is said to have enjoyed complaining.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme Jack Sprat could eat no fat, his wife could eat no lean, so Mrs Sprat literally liked to chew the fat.
explanation.definitionFit: In the rhyme the wife ate only fatty meat; as a British idiom the phrase means to chat at length or grumble.

clue.text: Left in shaft, it may produce light

indicators.note: in tells us the abbreviation for left is placed inside the word for shaft

parts.note: a cue is the long wooden shaft used in billiards or snooker

explanation.surface: Something left down a mine shaft might give off light.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'light' in crosswords is an answer slot in the grid, so a clue is what produces one.
explanation.definitionFit: Solving a crossword clue fills in a grid entry, which crossword setters call a light.

clue.text: Talked wittily — isn't it called cracking?

indicators.note: cracking means breaking up, so the letters of these words are broken and rearranged

explanation.surface: Asking whether a run of witty remarks is called wisecracking.
explanation.definitionFit: To scintillate is to sparkle, especially to be brilliantly clever in conversation.

clue.text: She's learned what a laundress might be doing about'. a neckcloth

indicators.note: about here means going round, so the laundry word wraps the neckcloth

parts.words: what a laundress might be doing
parts.note: blueing is rinsing white linen with blue dye to whiten it, a laundress's task
a stock is a wide cravat or neckcloth

explanation.surface: Wondering about an educated woman and a washerwoman busy with a cravat.
explanation.walkthrough: Blueing (also spelt bluing) was the old laundry rinse that kept white linen bright; 'She's learned' stands for a learned woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A bluestocking is an intellectual or literary woman, someone highly educated.

clue.text: "Run", they say, "See us being offensive"

indicators.note: they say means the word for run is spoken and only its sound is used

parts.note: to scurry is to run with short quick steps
lo is an old word meaning see or look
taken as written

explanation.surface: People shouting at someone to run off and come and look at their rudeness.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the sound of SCURRY is kept, spelt SCURRI; 'See' is the old exclamation LO.
explanation.definitionFit: Scurrilous means grossly abusive and insulting.

clue.text: In England Christmas for one lasts six hours

explanation.surface: An English festive holiday that seems to last only six hours.
explanation.walkthrough: The quarter days are the four days in England when rent was traditionally due; Christmas Day is one. A quarter of a 24-hour day is six hours.
explanation.definitionFit: Christmas Day is one of England's four rent-paying days; a quarter of a day is literally six hours.

clue.text: Invite vehicle to reverse in an, enclosed space

parts.note: to court is to invite or seek, as in courting disaster

indicators.note: to reverse tells us the word for the vehicle is written backwards

parts.note: a dray is a low cart, as used by brewers

explanation.surface: Asking a driver to back their car into a walled yard.
explanation.definitionFit: A courtyard is an open area surrounded by walls or buildings.

clue.text: One glance is enough to make us conform with English ways

indicators.note: enough to make us implies the letters are made over into something new

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A single look is all it takes to make us adopt English customs.
explanation.definitionFit: To anglicise is to make or become English in form or character.

clue.text: The champion loses his head when it's dark

indicators.note: losing the head means the first letter of the champion word is dropped

parts.note: a knight was a champion who fought on another's behalf

explanation.surface: A hero is beheaded once darkness falls.
explanation.definitionFit: Night is the time between dusk and dawn, the dark hours.

clue.text: It's not so common to see a bit of land between two rivers

indicators.note: between means the piece of land sits in the middle of the two rivers

parts.note: R is the usual abbreviation for river
R is the usual abbreviation for river, used a second time
an are is a metric unit of land area, 100 square metres

explanation.surface: Land squeezed between two rivers is a rare sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Rarer is the comparative of rare, meaning less often met with.

clue.text: Leaving without a second drink, giving rise to a lot of talk

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the leaving word goes round the rest

parts.note: going means leaving, departing
S is the abbreviation for second
a sip is a small drink

explanation.surface: Someone who walks out without finishing a quick drink sets tongues wagging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of 'outside'; it does not mean 'lacking'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gossiping, as a noun, is idle chatter about other people's affairs.

clue.text: In time girl gets the message and : cannot be got rid of

parts.note: taken as written
an era is a period of time
Di is a short girl's name, from Diana
a cable is a telegram, a message

explanation.surface: Eventually a young woman receives news that cannot be shaken off.
explanation.definitionFit: Ineradicable means impossible to remove or wipe out.

clue.text: Cause of trouble for king in the past

indicators.note: in means the king's letters are placed inside the word for the past

parts.note: ago means in the past
GR is Georgius Rex, King George

explanation.surface: A remark that there was strife for a monarch in former times.
explanation.definitionFit: Aggro is British slang for aggressive trouble-making or hassle.

clue.text: Board? It's above board, by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it tells us the honest-dealing word is spoken and heard as the answer

parts.note: above board means honest, fair

explanation.surface: A puzzled query about whether a committee is honest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' is not a committee but meals provided, as in board and lodging.
explanation.definitionFit: Fare is food provided, as in bed and board.

clue.text: One employed in munitions.

indicators.note: employed in means the letters are found used within the word

explanation.surface: A worker at an arms factory.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit is a single thing, a one.

clue.text: The probability of disaster doesn't scare our leaders

indicators.note: the leaders of these words are their first letters, read in order

explanation.surface: A claim that the chance of catastrophe leaves those in power unworried.
explanation.definitionFit: Odds are the ratio expressing how likely something is to happen.

clue.text: Investors used to employ it and agree in its involvement

indicators.note: involvement suggests the letters are tangled up together and rearranged

explanation.surface: A note about financiers who once used something and agreed to be part of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Investors' are not financiers but besiegers: to invest a town is to surround it with troops.
explanation.definitionFit: A siege train was the artillery and equipment an army brought to besiege a fortified place.

clue.text: River comes to a stop, we hear

indicators.note: we hear means the word for halting is spoken and sounds like the answer

parts.note: something that sticks jams and stops moving

explanation.surface: A river's flow is heard grinding to a halt.
explanation.definitionFit: The Styx is the mythological river of the Greek underworld.

clue.text: Time at the top? It never comes for him

parts.note: a second is a short unit of time
being at the top means being the best

explanation.surface: Some people never get their moment of glory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' in the definition refers back to 'Time at the top': the runner-up never gets to be first.
explanation.definitionFit: A second-best person is the runner-up, someone who never wins the top place.
